teaches: One thing against another: open on the difference that decides it; each side in its own terms; then why the difference has the consequence it has; land on a concrete fact, never on which to choose or what to do.

packet.title: Bacteria and viruses compared
sentences: A bacterium is a complete living cell, with a cell wall, its own machinery for making energy and proteins, and its own DNA.
Given warmth and nutrients a bacterium divides in two, and some species do so about every twenty minutes.
Most bacteria are harmless, and trillions live in the human gut, where many help with digestion.
Bacteria cause illness by multiplying where they should not be or by releasing toxins.
A virus is genetic material inside a protein shell, around a hundred times smaller than a bacterium.
A virus cannot grow or copy itself outside a living cell.
A virus enters a host cell and uses the cell's machinery to make copies of itself, which then spread to neighbouring cells.
Strep throat is caused by bacteria, and the common cold is caused by a virus.

packet.title: How antibiotics, antivirals and vaccines work
sentences: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, disrupts the bacterial cell wall, so the cell swells and bursts.
Other antibiotics block the machinery bacteria use to make proteins, which differs from the machinery in human cells.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses, which have no cell wall and no protein machinery of their own.
Antiviral drugs are harder to develop because a virus copies itself inside human cells, so stopping it risks harming the cell.
Tamiflu blocks the protein that influenza uses to release itself from an infected cell, and it works only against influenza.
One antibiotic can work against dozens of species of bacteria, while an antiviral usually works against one virus or one family.
A vaccine trains the immune system, which attacks both bacteria and viruses.
There are childhood vaccines against whooping cough, which is caused by a bacterium, and measles, which is caused by a virus.
An antibiotic taken during a viral infection still kills susceptible bacteria in the body and leaves resistant ones to multiply.
Anyone with a sore throat that lasts more than a week should see a doctor.
Researchers expect new classes of antibiotic to reach clinics in the coming decade.
Viruses were first seen under an electron microscope in the nineteen-thirties.
